A map of research questions about costs and limits

The small grid has eight filled cells. Group them into larger blocks. The total stays eight, but the view no longer shows the arrangement inside each block.

A summary can be useful without preserving every detail. The research asks a harder question: which rules and measurements remain reliable when the scale changes? The grid is an example of information loss, not a proof about physics.

Combine the cells into bigger blocks. Look for what stays the same and what disappears.

Words used here
coarse-graining
Combining small details into larger groups. This can preserve a total while losing information about the parts.
Read the fuller explanation

The illustration groups a fixed set of small cells into larger blocks. Totals remain available while the arrangement within each block is hidden. The view changes resolution; the underlying small pattern does not magically reorganize itself.

The research programme asks a harder version: whether admissibility, dynamics and identifying records remain consistent across declared scale maps. A finite calculation does not supply a regulator-, volume- or time-uniform theorem.

Follow the same quantity across the views. Then name one distinction you can no longer recover. A macro description can be useful without retaining every microscopic answer.

A map of research questions about costs and limits

Asks what a result costs, what measurement changes, and which conclusions survive a change of scale. Many questions remain open.

Cost, backaction, scale and rare events

Separates convergence from resource cost, conditioned trajectories from unconditional channels, and finite calculations from scale-uniform control. The rate table in the reader comes from the documented four-mode virtual experiment; it is numerical evidence in that authored model.
